---
title: "Imitating a Class in Rust: `struct` + `impl` (+ `trait`)"
---

Rust has no `class` keyword. The pieces of a class are split across separate language features:

```
          C# / Python "class"                         Rust
 ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────────┐
 │  fields (data)               │  ───►  │  struct      { fields }       │
 │  constructor                 │  ───►  │  impl  →  fn new() -> Self    │
 │  methods                     │  ───►  │  impl  →  fn m(&self, ...)    │
 │  static methods              │  ───►  │  impl  →  fn f(...) (no self) │
 │  private / public            │  ───►  │  mod + pub (module-level)     │
 │  interface / abstract class  │  ───►  │  trait                        │
 │  inheritance                 │  ───►  │  ✗ none → composition + trait │
 │  destructor / IDisposable    │  ───►  │  impl Drop                    │
 └──────────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────────┘
```

Data and behavior are declared separately, then joined by `impl`.

---

## 1. A basic "class"

Here is a familiar C# class:

```csharp
public class BankAccount {
    private string owner;
    private long balance;
    public BankAccount(string owner) { this.owner = owner; balance = 0; }
    public void Deposit(long amount) { balance += amount; }
    public long Balance => balance;
}
```

This is the Rust equivalent:

```rust
pub struct BankAccount {
    owner: String,   // fields are private by default
    balance: i64,
}

impl BankAccount {
    /// "Constructor": just a regular associated function by convention named `new`
    pub fn new(owner: &str) -> Self {
        Self { owner: owner.to_string(), balance: 0 }
    }

    /// Getter: borrows self read-only
    pub fn balance(&self) -> i64 {
        self.balance
    }

    /// Mutating method: borrows self mutably
    pub fn deposit(&mut self, amount: i64) {
        self.balance += amount;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut acc = BankAccount::new("KS");   // `::` calls an associated fn
    acc.deposit(100);                       // `.` calls a method
    println!("{}", acc.balance());          // 100
}
```

There are a few things to notice. `Self` is an alias for the type being implemented (`BankAccount`). `new` is not special to the compiler. It's only a convention, so you can have `new`, `with_owner`, `from_csv`, and so on, which works like named constructors. The variable must be declared `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method, because Rust makes mutability explicit at the binding site.

---

## 2. The three kinds of `self`

This part has no direct equivalent in C# or Python. It's where Rust's ownership system enters OOP.

```
 Receiver     Meaning                     Caller still owns obj?   Can mutate?
 ─────────    ─────────────────────────   ──────────────────────   ───────────
 &self        borrow read-only            ✅ yes                    ❌
 &mut self    borrow exclusively          ✅ yes                    ✅
 self         take ownership (consume)    ❌ no — moved             ✅
 (none)       associated fn ("static")    n/a                      n/a
```

A consuming method is useful for "finalizing" an object:

```rust
impl BankAccount {
    /// Closes the account and returns the remaining money.
    /// After this, the account no longer exists.
    pub fn close(self) -> i64 {
        self.balance
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut acc = BankAccount::new("KS");
    acc.deposit(50);
    let cash = acc.close();
    // acc.deposit(10);   // ❌ compile error: value moved in `close`
}
```

The compiler enforces "you can't use a closed account". In C#, you would need a runtime `ObjectDisposedException` check for that.

**Rule of thumb:** default to `&self`. Use `&mut self` only when you modify fields. Use `self` for transformations or builders that hand back a new value.

---

## 3. Encapsulation: privacy is per module, not per class

In C#, `private` means "only this class can see it". In Rust, private means "only this module (and its children) can see it".

```rust
mod bank {
    pub struct BankAccount {
        pub owner: String,  // public field
        balance: i64,       // private field
    }

    impl BankAccount {
        pub fn new(owner: &str) -> Self {
            Self { owner: owner.to_string(), balance: 0 }
        }
        pub fn balance(&self) -> i64 { self.balance }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let acc = bank::BankAccount::new("KS");
    println!("{}", acc.owner);        // ✅ pub field
    // println!("{}", acc.balance);   // ❌ private field
    // let fake = bank::BankAccount { owner: "x".into(), balance: 999 };
    //                                // ❌ can't build it: a field is private
}
```

```
 ┌──────────── mod bank ────────────┐
 │  struct BankAccount              │   Everything inside `bank`
 │     owner   (pub)  ──────────────┼──► visible outside
 │     balance (private)            │   can see `balance`.
 │  impl BankAccount { ... }        │
 │  fn audit(a: &BankAccount) {     │   ← even this free function
 │      a.balance  // ✅ allowed     │     can read it (same module)
 │  }                               │
 └──────────────────────────────────┘
```

Having one private field also means outsiders must use your constructor. That's how you enforce invariants, like "balance is never negative".

---

## 4. Error handling instead of exceptions

Methods that can fail return a `Result` instead of throwing:

```rust
impl BankAccount {
    pub fn withdraw(&mut self, amount: i64) -> Result<(), String> {
        if amount > self.balance {
            return Err(format!("Insufficient funds: have {}", self.balance));
        }
        self.balance -= amount;
        Ok(())
    }
}

// usage
match acc.withdraw(500) {
    Ok(()) => println!("done"),
    Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
}
```

---

## 5. Interfaces and polymorphism: `trait`

A `trait` is like a C# `interface`, and it can have default method bodies, like a base class's virtual method.

```rust
trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;                    // required (abstract)

    fn describe(&self) -> String {            // default (like a virtual method)
        format!("Shape with area {:.2}", self.area())
    }
}

struct Circle { r: f64 }
struct Rect   { w: f64, h: f64 }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { std::f64::consts::PI * self.r * self.r }
}

impl Shape for Rect {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.w * self.h }
    fn describe(&self) -> String {            // "override"
        format!("Rectangle {}x{}", self.w, self.h)
    }
}
```

There are two ways to use polymorphism:

```rust
// (A) Static dispatch — generics, resolved at compile time (zero cost)
fn print_area(s: &impl Shape) {
    println!("{}", s.area());
}

// (B) Dynamic dispatch — trait objects, vtable at runtime (like C# virtual)
fn main() {
    let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![
        Box::new(Circle { r: 1.0 }),
        Box::new(Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }),
    ];
    for s in &shapes {
        println!("{}", s.describe());
    }
}
```

```
 Static (impl Shape / <T: Shape>)        Dynamic (dyn Shape)
 ───────────────────────────────         ──────────────────────────
 compiler copies fn per type             one fn, lookup via vtable
 fastest, inlinable                      tiny runtime cost
 one concrete type per call              mixed types in one Vec ✅
```

Use (B) whenever you need a heterogeneous list. That's the classic `List<IShape>` situation.

---

## 6. No inheritance → composition

Rust deliberately has no `class Dog : Animal`. You compose structs and share behavior through traits. This is the "favor composition over inheritance" principle, enforced by the language.

```rust
struct Engine { hp: u32 }

struct Car {
    brand: String,
    engine: Engine,          // HAS-A instead of IS-A
}

impl Car {
    fn horsepower(&self) -> u32 {
        self.engine.hp       // explicit delegation
    }
}
```

```
 Inheritance (C#)              Composition + Trait (Rust)
 ─────────────────             ───────────────────────────
      Animal                    trait Speak { fn speak(&self); }
        ▲                              ▲            ▲
   ┌────┴────┐                    impl for Dog  impl for Cat
  Dog       Cat                 (each struct independent;
 (inherits fields + methods)     shared contract, no shared state)
```

---

## 7. "Built-in" class features through standard traits

Many things that C# gives every object come from standard traits you derive or implement:

```rust
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Default)]   // auto-generated impls
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

impl fmt::Display for Point {                 // ≈ override ToString()
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "({}, {})", self.x, self.y)
    }
}

impl Drop for Point {                         // ≈ destructor / Dispose()
    fn drop(&mut self) { println!("dropping {self}"); }
}
```

| C# concept | Rust equivalent |
|---|---|
| `ToString()` override | `impl Display` |
| debugger view | `#[derive(Debug)]` → `{:?}` |
| `Equals` / `==` | `#[derive(PartialEq)]` |
| parameterless ctor | `#[derive(Default)]` → `Point::default()` |
| copy constructor / `MemberwiseClone` | `#[derive(Clone)]` → `.clone()` |
| destructor / `IDisposable` | `impl Drop` (runs automatically and deterministically at scope end) |
| `partial class` | multiple `impl` blocks for the same type |

---

## Mental model summary

```
   struct   = WHAT the object is      (state)
   impl     = WHAT it can do          (behavior, bound to one type)
   trait    = WHAT it promises        (contract, shared across types)
   mod/pub  = WHO can see it          (encapsulation)
   &self / &mut self / self = HOW it is accessed (ownership-aware OOP)
```

The biggest shift from C# or Python is that ownership is part of every method's signature. Once you read `&self`, `&mut self`, and `self` as "look", "modify", and "consume", Rust "classes" start feeling natural.
